list.listitem: Restlessness, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, aural fullness, and conjunctival injection make the diagnosis of cluster headache (CH) more likely, as well as excruciating pain; unilateral pain; location of pain near eyes, temples or teeth; duration of attacks less than 3 to 4 hours; and attacks for at least 7 days in a row, make CH less likely. C

Recommended first-line treatments for acute CH include 100% oxygen (6-12 L/min) via non-rebreather face mask, intranasal zolmitriptan (5 or 10 mg), or SC sumatriptan (6 mg).Oxygen, which is highly effective, may not be routinely available with Medcaid or MediCare and may require physician advocacy to access this effective treatment for patients. A
Options for maintenance prophylaxis include intranasal civamide (100 mcg daily), suboccipital steroid injections B and verapamil (360 mg),
Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-targeted medication is under investigation. They have been demonstrated effective for episdodic CH.B
Deep-brain hypothalamic stimulation may be an effective option for patients with chronic cluster headache not responsive to medical therapy. B

background.definition: Cluster headache (CH) is a severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes accompanied by at least one of the following: ipsilateral conjunctival injection or lacrimation, nasal congestion or rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, forehead and facial sweating, miosis or ptosis, restlessness or agitation. At least five attacks must have occurred at a frequency from one every other day to eight per day, and separated by periods of pain-free remission. CH is a type of Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalagia (TAC). These disorders present with trigeminal pain and autonomic symptoms and share a common pathophysiology involving the trigemrminovascular system.

list.listitem: About 1/1000 persons or 0.1% to 0.2% of the population, of whom 10% have chronic CH.

CH is an inherited disorder in a subset of families. Authors of a systematic review of 40 papers found a median positive family history rate of CH of 8.2% with a range of 0% to 22%; in the 5 largest studies, there was a positive family history rate of 18%. Most pedigrees (46 of 67 [69%]) were consistent with an autosomal dominant pattern and 28% were consistent with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. In another systematic review, the estimated rate of family history in CH was similar at 6.27% (95% CI: 4.65-8.40%).
Eight to ten percent of people present with headache.
CH is commonly described as the most severe type of headache.

In one cohort study of patients with CH, male to female ratio was 6.2 to 1 with headache onset in the 1960s, but decreased to 2.1 to 1 with onset in the 1990s. A pooled data study suggests a ratio of 4.3 to 1, with males much more predominant in cases of chronic CH (ratio 15 to 1).

The ratio of male/femaie has recently been identified as lower than previously recognized.The diagnosis has often been missed in women, perhaps because of misdiagnosis of migraine, co-morbidity of migraine headache, and misdiagnosis of symptoms.
For men, peak age of onset is in their 40s; may start in 20s. For women, peak age onset is in their 60s.

Many patients with CH report symptoms of depression, including suicidal thoughts, essentially grieving the loss of their previous life, and coping with the burden of the pain and disability of living with CH. In a web-based US survey of 1134 individuals with CH, over half (55%) reported having had suicidal ideation.
In addition, 20% of the patients in the US survey lost a job due to CH and 8% were out of work or on disability from CH.
Abnormality of autonomic function with increased parasympathetic drive and decreased sympathetic function.
Disorder of circadian rhythm.
Periods of reduced oxygenation during sleep can trigger an attack (increased incidence of sleep apnea in patients with CH).
Variable methionine-enkephalin levels (an opioid mediator in the brain) may be a possible treatment target.
Pathophysiology is poorly understood and appears to involve the hypothalamic gray matter.
For some, an autosomal dominant gene is involved.
It may involve an abnormality of autonomic function with increased parasympathetic drive and decreased sympathetic function or disorder of circadian rhythm.
Periods of reduced oxygenation during sleep may trigger an attack (increased incidence of sleep apnea in CH patients).

Calcitionin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a strong vasodilator found in trigeminal neurons and plays a key role in CH. CGRP is released during a CH attack and, if CGRP is given to a CH patient during an active period, it will precipitate a CH attack.
Verapamil 240 to 480 mg daily reduces the number of attacks in a cluster period and is recommended for prophylaxis. A

Verapamil is best taken in three divided doses. It may be better to give a larger dose at night about 2 hours before the usual time of headache onset. Verapamil may be more effective in men than women. B

Lithium (causes frequent side effects) and topiramate are alternatives for prophylaxis but are not as well studied as verapamil. C Patients should be closely monitored for side effects and, in the case of lithium, blood levels should be obtained. In addition, it is not advisable to combine these drugs with the acute use of triptans.

Authors of a systematic review rated intranasal civamide (100 mcg daily)( similar to capsaicin) or suboccipital steroid injections useful for prevention of CH, B and verapamil (360 mg), lithium (900 mg), and melatonin (10 mg) as possibly useful. C

Galcanezumab, a monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to CGRP, has been reported effective and well tolerated in phase III trials for preventive treatment of migraine headache and episodic CH, and received FDA approval.B

A systematic review identified 2 RCTs and 16 observational studies of greater occipital nerve (GON) block to prevent CT. They concluded that the procedure is effective and safe, and that likelihood of serious adverse events could be reduced by using methylprednisolone.
A randomized trial with 231 adults found that eptinezumab was not effective for prevention of cluster headache.
Diagnosis is primarily made by history; unilateral pain, excruciating pain, restlessness, and short duration (<3-4 hour) are the most accurate symptoms. C

Imaging studies (preferably MRI or CT scan with contrast and LP if sub-arachnoid headache is suspected) should be ordered for patients with new, severe headache, neurologic findings on examination, a change in headache pattern, or other red flags for serious intracranial disease. C

Differential.Differential_Name: SUNCT headache (short-acting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing) (type of TAC)
Differential.Differential_Features: 15-120 sec episodes of stabbing, throbbing pain, 5-6 attacks/hour with autonomic features

Differential.Differential_Name: Hemicrania continua (related to TAC, but different category)
Differential.Differential_Features: Responds to indomethacin, more common in females; unilateral, mild chronic baseline, less severe
Atypical presentation suggests need for additional workup
Female predominance, bilateral, no autonomic features, but occurs nightly in rapid eye movement sleep

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: The International Headache Society defines CH as at least five severe to very several unilateral headaches lasting 15-180 minutes if untreated, and accompanied by at least one of the following ipsilateral to the headache: conjunctival injection and/or lacrimation, nasal congestion and/or rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, forehead and facial sweating, and miosis and /or ptosis; AND/OR a sense of restlessness or agitation (people find it difficult to stay still). CH occur at a frequency between one every other day to 8 daily and are not better accounted for by another diagnosis.

list.listitem: Consider cluster headache in patients with excruciating uniateral headache with autonomic symptoms and restlesssness, which often occurs at night.
Cluster headache (CH) is often misdiagnosed; the average diagnostic delay is 5 to 7 years. Only 21% of patients with CH were diagnosed at the first visit in one cohort study.

The most sensitive predictors of CH, present in almost all patients with the condition, are excruciating pain; unilateral pain; location of pain near eyes, temples or teeth; duration of attacks less than 3 to 4 hours; and attacks for at least 7 days in a row. Their absence makes the diagnosis unlikely.
Highly specific findings include restlessness, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and conjunctival injection. Their presence makes the diagnosis more likely.
Unilateral lacrimation is present in 90% of patients.

In a US survey, reported triggers included smells, weather changes, and alcohol, especially beer. Additional reported triggers include vasodilators (e.g., alcohol, nitroglycerin, carbon dioxide), smoking, and sildenafil.Additional reported triggers include watching telelvision, hot weather, stress, sexual activity.
CH may be episodic or chronic (i.e., attacks may recur over more than 1 year without remission periods or with remission periods lasting <1 month).

A study comparing CH symptoms in males and females noted that ptosis and nasal congestion were more likely in women than men, as were osmophobia and nausea. The onset of disease in women often correlated with moments of important changes in the levels of sexual hormones (e.g. menarche, post-partum, at menopasue).
There are no specific diagnostic tests for CH.

Imaging studies (preferably MRI or CT scan with contrast and LP if sub-arachnoid headache is suspected) should be ordered for patients with new, severe headache, neurologic findings on examination, a change in headache pattern, or other red flags for serious intracranial disease (e.g., headache triggered by cough or exertion; change in mental status; new headache in a patients with cancer, HIV or Lyme disease; meningismus; papilledema).
Rule out pituitary abnormality, patients with prolactinomas and growth hormone tumors may present with TAC's
Patients with CH who have a BMI greater than 25 kg/m2 and are older than 40 years of age are recommended to have a sleep study to assess for sleep apnea.

A study of 71 patients in a headache clinic found that the combination of unilateral pain plus at least 5 of 7 other key symptoms (excruciating pain, location near eye or temple, rhinorrhea, duration less than 3 to 4 hours, more than one attack on the same day, and attacks for at least 7 consecutive days) was 100% sensitive and 95% specific for CH.
When applying this combination to a group with a 25% pretest probability of CH, 87% of patients meeting these criteria had CH compared with only 0.3% of those who did not meet the criteria.
CH should be considered in any patient with severe, unilateral headache.
Imaging studies are recommended to rule out serious intracranial pathology in patients with red flags such as new onset headache, change in headache, or abnormal neurologic examination.
Test for sleep apnea in patients over age 40 years who are overweight and/or if indicated by history.
Verapamil is the first-line drug for prophylaxis.
Oxygen is a first-line acute treatment that is effective in 75% of patients, without side effects and underutilized, in part due to lack of insurance coverage for at-home use.
Triptans are also first-line treatments if there are no contraindications (e.g., smoking, heart disease).

Empathy, compassion, and a long-term trusted relationship with a clinician is important, especially in conditions with severe symptoms like CH. Diagnosis often does not occur for 6-7 years and patients may have been searching for help for a long time.
If initial treatments are not effective, keep working with the patient to explore other treatment modalities and consider consultation with a specialist in CH.
Patients should avoid triggers such as alcohol, smoking, shift work, glare, staring at TV or other screens. C
100% oxygen 6 to 12 L per minute for 15 minutes via non-rebreather face mask is the treatment of choice for acute CH. A
Intranasal zolmitriptan and SC sumatriptan may be effective for acute CH. A
Subcutaneous (SC) sumatriptan may be more effective than intranasal zolmitriptan for rapid action .
The use of prednisone (60 mg to 100 mg/day for 5 days then tapering by 10 mg/day) is an option during acute attacks but is based on limited clinical trial data. B
Verapamil 240 to 480 mg per day is recommended as first-line therapy for maintenance. As in

Intranasal zolmitriptan (5 mg or 10 mg) and sumatriptan 6 mg SC are effective for acute headaches. Contraindicated in patients with cardiac or cerebrovascular disease (for these patients, start with oxygen treatment).F

Based on limited data, SC sumatriptan 6 mg was superior to intranasal zolmitriptan 5 mg or 10 mg for rapid (15 minute) responses, which are important in this condition. Oral routes of administration are not appropriate based on a 2018 Cochrane review.

Sumatriptan nasal spray 20 mg and oral zolmitriptan 5 and 10 mg are also likely effective, but evidence is less robust. Contraindicated in patients with cardiac or cerebrovascular disease (for these patients, start with oxygen treatment).
The most common side effects of triptans are nausea, fatigue, paresthesias, chest/throat tightness, and unpleasant taste.
Octreotide SC 100 µg can be used in patients with cardiovascular diseases. Side effects include hypoglycemia.
Lidocaine (intranasal 1 mL [4%-10%]) is only moderately effective for head pain.

Prednisone (60-100 mg per day for 5 days, then tapering) can be used during acute attacks based on limited clinical trial data, and as transitional prophylaxis. Prednisone is started simultaneously with a maintenance prophylaxis drug such as verapamil.

There is insuffcient supporting evidence for prednisone 20 mg every other day as effective ongoing prevention. There is also insufficient evidence that prednisone 30 mg acutely is effective for acute cluster headache.

A trial randomized 106 patients to the monoclonal antibody galcanezumab or placebo at baseline and one month later as an injection. At baseline both groups had 17.3 to 17.8 cluster headaches per week. This was reduced by 8.7 in the treatment grou3p and 5.2 in the placebo group. At least a 50% reduction was seen more often in the treatment group (71% vs 53%, p = 0.046, NNT = 5).
Hypothalamic stimulation using deep-brain electrodes is effective for the treatment of chronic CH refractory to other forms of therapy.

Occipital nerve stimulation may also be an effective treatment for chronic refractory CH. However, treatment may be less effective than for other types of headache and it may take several months to show an effect.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 studies including two RCTs of occipital nerve blocks for the treatment of CH found a pooled proportion of pain-free subjects at 1 month of 50% (95% CI 24% to 76%) with considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 88%). Combining only the results of the 2 RCTs, the relative risk ratio of pain freedom at 1 month in active vs. control groups was 4.86, 95% CI 1.35-17.55.

Transcutaneuos non-invasive vagal nerve stimulation (nVNS) has been FDA approved and is being used in episdodic and preventive treatment, especially in patients with chronic CH. Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 trials with 983 patients found nVNS more effective than sham-device treatment for achieving a pain-free status within 30 minutes (OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.2 to 4.4), pain-relief status within 30 and at 60 minutes, reduction in abortive medication use (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.92), and pain-free status in more than half of treated attacks but no difference in headache days, adverse events or satisfaction.

In a sham-controlled RCT of 93 patients with chronic CH, sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation via an implanted device resulted in greater likelihood of pain relief at 15 minutes (62% vs 39%, OR 2.6, 95% CI 1.3-5.3, NNT = 4).
A small RCT (n=40) concluded that greater occipital nerve block with methylprednisolone 80 mg and lidocaine was more effective than placebo at reducing attack frequency over a 4 week period.
Trigeminal radiosurgery for refractory CH is NOT an effective treatment. In fact, complete resection of the trigeminal nerve does not reduce headache frequency.
Melatonin has been proposed as an adjunctive therapy (melatonin levels are lower than usual during CH attacks), but a small crossover trial with 9 patients found no benefit.
Botox injections have been proposed but not studied in randomized trials. Significant improvement in CH frequency was demonstrated in several small case series.

Intranasal capsaicin (0.025% on cotton-tipped applicator twice a day in ipsilateral nostril for 7 days) was effective in reducing attack severity and frequency and may also be tried as an adjunct. The major side effect was intense local discomfort.

Authors of a systematic review found two small clinical trials of hyperbaric oxygen therapy for CH; one trial demonstrated a trend toward better outcomes compared with sham therapy but was underpowered.
Boswellia Serratia (Indian frankincense) in an open label uncontrolled study improved symptoms in chronic CH in 4 patients.

Normobaric oxygen, 100% at 6 to 12 L per minute for 15 minutes via face mask is the treatment of choice for acute CH. A About 75% of patients will respond to this treatment. Patients should be sitting up, using a non-rebreather mask, and flow can be increased to 15 L and adjusted per patient. No major side effects have been reported and oxygen therapy is not contraindicated in patients with cardiac or cerebrovascular disease.It is quite important for physicians to advocate for this treatment for their patients since MediCaid and MediCare do not routinely cover this highly effectdive treatment with almost no side-effects.
If insurance refuses coverage, it is important to work with patients to find free or affordable sources of oxygen trreatment from community programs, free clinics, etc.
Cochrane authors found one negative trial of use of hyperbaric oxygen therapy for termination of CH, but the trial had low power.
Cognitive behavioral therapy can help with coping and fear but not necessarily with headaches.
Avoiding naps and changes in sleep patterns during an episode may also be of help. CH episodes often occur after prolonged periods of changes in sleep cycle (e.g., work shifts or travel).
Patients are also traditionally advised to avoid excessive heat and smells of gasoline and oil, which can also be triggers.
Oral sodium oxybate, a compound that consolidates sleep and increases slow-wave sleep, was helpful in 4 patients with CH.
Triggers, especially alcohol, should be avoided.
Predictors of progression from episodic to chronic CH include late onset, high frequency of cluster periods, short-lived remission periods, and the presence of sporadic (non-cluster) attacks. B
CH is very painful, but there are treatments. If the treatment received is not working, ask for another treatment and/or to see a neurologist who is an expert in CH.
